title: Wind Energy & Biogas Calculations
subtitle: Power in Wind, Digester Design & Community Gas Supply
learningOutcome: By the end of this week, you should be able to calculate air density from the ideal gas law, find total power, maximum power density, and torque for a wind turbine, design a family biogas digester from dung input to power output, and solve a village-scale community biogas plant for gas supply, demand balance, and digester dimensions.

content.text: Before calculating any wind power, you need to know the density of the air at your site. This might seem like a small detail but it is not — wind power is directly proportional to air density. Denser air carries more mass per cubic metre, and more mass means more kinetic energy per second flowing through the turbine blades.
Air density is not a fixed constant you memorise. It depends on pressure and temperature at the site. Your lecturer always derives it fresh from the ideal gas law.

content.name: Air Density (rho) — kg/m³
content.desc: Mass of air per unit volume. At sea level and 15°C, ρ ≈ 1.225 kg/m³. Cold air is denser (heavier molecules pack tighter). High-altitude air is less dense. For wind power calculations, always compute ρ from site pressure and temperature — do not assume 1.225 unless given standard conditions.

content.label: Air Density from Ideal Gas Law
content.note:
P = atmospheric pressure (Pa) — 1 atm = 1.01325 × 10⁵ Pa
R = specific gas constant for air = 0.287 kJ/kg·K = 287 J/kg·K
T = absolute temperature (Kelvin) = °C + 273

For standard conditions (1 atm, 15°C): ρ = 101325 ÷ (287 × 288) = 1.226 kg/m³

questions.question: Air density ρ is calculated from site pressure and temperature using which formula?
options: ρ = P · R · T
ρ = P / (R · T)
ρ = (R · T) / P
ρ = P² / (R · T)

questions.question: At 1 atm and 15°C standard conditions, air density evaluates to ________ kg/m³.

content.text: Your lecturer's wind turbine question always asks for five things in order. Understanding what each one is before calculating it is what separates someone who understands from someone who is guessing.

content.name: Total Power Density — W/m²
content.desc: The total kinetic energy flux through 1 m² of the air stream per second. This is the maximum possible power available in the wind — before the turbine extracts any of it.

content.label: Total Wind Power Density
content.note: V = wind speed (m/s). Power varies with V³ — doubling wind speed gives 8× more power.

content.name: Betz Limit = 59.3%
content.desc: The theoretical maximum fraction of wind power that any turbine can ever extract. Derived by Albert Betz in 1919.

content.label: Maximum Power Density (Betz Limit)
content.note: Note: 8/27 = 0.296, which is exactly (16/27)/2 — consistent with the Betz derivation.

content.label: Maximum Axial Thrust
content.note: The factor π/9 comes from the Betz derivation for the thrust coefficient.

content.title: Wind Turbine — D = 120m, V = 15 m/s, 40 rpm
given: Wind speed V = 15 m/s | Diameter D = 120m
Operating speed N = 40 rpm at max efficiency
Efficiency η = 35% | Gas constant R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K
content.result: ✓ Summary: ρ = 1.226 kg/m³ | P/A = 2,069 W/m² | Betz max = 1,226 W/m² | At 35%: 724 W/m² | Total P = 8,184 kW | Torque = 55,170 N·m | Axial thrust = 1,385,870 N

questions.question: If wind speed doubles from 10 m/s to 20 m/s, total wind power density increases by a factor of:
The theoretical maximum fraction of wind power any turbine can extract is ________%.
Why is axial thrust important to engineers designing a wind turbine tower?
questions.answer: Axial thrust is the horizontal pushing force the wind exerts on the rotor in the direction of wind flow. This force must be transmitted down through the tower into the foundation. For a 120m turbine at 15 m/s, this force is approximately 1.4 million Newtons — enough to topple the tower if the structure is not strong enough. Engineers use the axial thrust calculation to design tower wall thickness, guy-wires, and foundation size to safely resist this overturning force.

activeRecall.question: State the full calculation sequence for a wind turbine problem. What is calculated first and why?
activeRecall.answer:
1. ρ = P/RT — air density first. Everything else depends on it. Do not assume 1.225 — always derive from given P and T.

2. P/A = ½ρV³ — total power density. The maximum possible energy per m² of wind stream.

3. P/A = (8/27)ρV³ — Betz maximum. The physical ceiling no turbine can exceed.

4. P/A = η × ½ρV³ — realistic power density using given efficiency (35%).

5. P = (P/A) × πD²/4 — total power by multiplying density by swept area.

6. Torque and axial thrust formulas — mechanical forces on the structure.

questions.question: Why is air density derived from ρ = P/RT for every site?
options: 1.225 kg/m³ is only valid at sea level and 15°C — pressure and temperature vary by location
The ideal gas law makes air density constant everywhere
Air density changes with turbine rotational speed
Air density does not affect wind power calculations

questions.question: What is the maximum theoretical efficiency limit for any wind turbine rotor according to Betz?
Wind power density is proportional to the cube of ________.

topics.title: Family Biogas Digester — Design & Power Output

subtopics.title: What a Biogas Digester Actually Is

content.text: A biogas digester is an airtight sealed tank where organic waste — usually animal dung or agricultural residue — is mixed with water and left to ferment in the absence of oxygen. Bacteria inside break down the organic material and produce biogas as a by-product. The biogas (mostly methane) is piped off and burned for cooking or electricity.

The Mechanical Stomach Analogy: You feed organic waste in one end (daily input). The bacteria process it over several days (retention time). Gas comes out the top. Spent slurry comes out the bottom — this slurry is rich in nutrients and makes excellent fertiliser. Nothing is wasted.

questions.question: Explain how a biogas digester operates like a mechanical stomach.
questions.answer: Organic waste mixed with water enters daily (input), bacteria ferment it anaerobically over a fixed retention time (digestion), biogas is captured from the top for energy, and nutrient-rich slurry exits at the bottom as fertiliser.

subtopics.title: The Four Quantities — Input to Output

content.text: The family biogas calculation always follows the same four-step chain. Each step uses the result from the previous one.

content.name: Daily Dry Matter Input (kg/day)
content.desc: The mass of dry organic matter fed into the digester each day. For cattle dung: each cow produces about 2 kg of dry matter per day.

content.name: Daily Slurry Volume (m³/day)
content.desc: The volume of slurry entering the digester per day. Slurry density ρin = 50 kg/m³ is a standard design constant for cattle dung slurry.

content.label: Daily Slurry Volume
content.note: ρin = 50 kg/m³ (standard design constant for cattle dung slurry).

content.name: Retention Time (days)
content.desc: How long the organic material must remain inside the digester for complete fermentation. Typical value is 20 days.

content.label: Digester Volume
content.note: Vd = Vf × tr. The tank must hold tr days' worth of slurry simultaneously.

content.label: Daily Biogas Production
content.note: C = biogas yield (m³ per kg of dry matter). For cattle dung: C = 0.24 m³/kg.

content.label: Daily Power Available from Digester
content.note: η = burner efficiency (0.6), Hm = 28 MJ/m³, Fm = 0.8 (80% methane fraction), Vb = daily biogas volume.

content.title: Family Biogas Digester — 5 Cows, 20 Days Retention
given: 5 cows | dry matter per cow = 2 kg/day | retention time tr = 20 days
Slurry density ρin = 50 kg/m³ | Biogas yield C = 0.24 m³/kg
Methane fraction Fm = 0.8 (80%) | Burner efficiency η = 0.6 (60%)
Heat of combustion of methane Hm = 28 MJ/m³

steps.label: Step 5
steps.title: Daily energy output E and continuous thermal power

content.result: ✓ A 4 m³ digester fed by 5 cows produces 2.4 m³ of biogas per day, delivering 32.25 MJ/day — equivalent to a 373W heater running 24 hours a day.

questions.question: The retention time of 20 days means:
options: Gas is produced for 20 days then the digester is emptied
The digester must be refilled every 20 days
Each batch of slurry must remain inside the digester for 20 days for complete fermentation
It takes 20 days from installation before gas production starts

questions.question: Why is the methane fraction Fm needed in the power formula?
questions.answer: Biogas is a mixture (60–80% CH₄, 20–40% CO₂). Only the methane fraction burns and releases heat — CO₂ is inert. Fm selects only the combustible methane fraction so power is not overestimated.

activeRecall.question: State the 5-step chain for a family biogas digester problem.
activeRecall.answer:
1. mo = animals × kg/day per animal → daily dry matter input

2. Vf = mo / ρin → daily slurry volume

3. Vd = Vf × tr → digester volume

4. Vb = C × mo → daily biogas production

5. E = η × Hm × Fm × Vb → daily useful energy output.

questions.question: What is the primary factor that determines the required volume of a family digester Vd?
options: Daily slurry volume Vf multiplied by retention time tr
Biogas volume Vb multiplied by burner efficiency η
Atmospheric pressure P at the site
Rotor diameter D of the feeding mixer

questions.question: Why does carbon dioxide in biogas contribute zero combustion heat?
options: It is fully oxidised and non-combustible
It turns into liquid methane when burned
It evaporates before reaching the burner
It absorbs all heat released by methane

questions.question: In Worked Example 9.2, 5 cows produce a daily dry matter input mo of ________ kg/day.

topics.title: Village Community Biogas Plant — Supply, Demand & Digester Sizing

subtopics.title: The Big Picture — Supply vs Demand Logic

content.text: The village biogas problem is bigger than the family digester, but the logic is the same — just scaled up and with an important extra step: you must verify that your supply of gas meets your community's demand before sizing the digesters.

Why Design for Winter? Gas production from biogas digesters slows in cold weather because bacterial activity decreases at lower temperatures. Winter yield = 42 litres/kg vs summer yield = 55 litres/kg. You must design the plant to meet demand during winter — the worst case.

questions.question: Why is the village biogas plant designed based on winter gas yield?
options: Gas demand is highest in winter
Bacterial activity slows down in winter giving the lowest (worst-case) gas yield per kg of dung
Dung supply is lowest in winter
Water freezes in summer

content.text: Once the number of digesters is chosen (e.g. 4 digesters), each digester is sized by calculating daily charge volume, applying retention time, adding a 10% safety margin, and solving for H = D geometry.

content.name: Slurry Density for Village Digesters — kg/m³
content.desc: In community plants, dung is mixed 1:1 with water by mass. The resulting slurry density is 1090 kg/m³.

content.label: Volume of Daily Charge per Digester
Digester Dimensions (H = D for large plants)

content.title: Village Biogas Plant — 98 Families, Mixed Livestock
given: 98 families (490 total persons) | 102 cows, 124 oxen, 52 buffalo, 3 pigs
Winter yield: 42 L/kg | Retention time tr = 30 days | 4 digesters | H = D
content.result: ✓ Each of the 4 digesters has diameter D = 4m and height H = 4m. Winter gas supply (138.6 m³/day) satisfies demand (136.92 m³/day).

questions.question: In the digester volume formula, why is a 10% safety factor (1.1 multiplier) applied?
questions.answer: The 10% safety factor accounts for minor gas/slurry leakage, minor population/livestock growth, measurement uncertainties in dung supply, and demand fluctuations.

activeRecall.question: State the full sequence for a village biogas plant problem from animal census to digester dimensions.
activeRecall.answer:
1. Total dung: sum dung across all animal species.
2. Gas supply: dung × winter yield (litres/kg) converted to m³/day.
3. Gas demand: cooking + lighting.
4. Verify supply > demand.
5. Dung per digester: total dung ÷ number of digesters.
6. Daily charge volume: (dung + equal water) ÷ 1090 kg/m³.
7. Digester volume: 1.1 × daily charge × 30 days.
8. Dimensions: D = (V / 0.785)^(1/3), H = D.

questions.question: What is the slurry density used for village biogas digesters where dung is mixed 1:1 with water?
options: 50 kg/m³
1000 kg/m³
1090 kg/m³
1226 kg/m³

questions.question: If height H equals diameter D for a cylindrical tank, what is the formula for volume in terms of D?
options: V = π D²
V = (π/4) D³
V = 2 π D³
V = π D³ / 3

questions.question: In Worked Example 9.3, each of the 4 village digesters has a diameter D of ________ metres.
Why is air density always calculated from ρ = P/RT rather than assumed as 1.225 kg/m³?
options: 1.225 kg/m³ is only valid at the equator
The ideal gas law gives a more accurate value of exactly 1.225 kg/m³
Air density depends on site temperature and pressure — it varies and must be derived from given conditions
The ideal gas law accounts for wind speed

feedback.correct: Correct. Air density depends on site temperature and pressure — always derive it from given conditions.
feedback.wrong: Incorrect. ρ = P/RT because air density varies with temperature and pressure. Never assume 1.225 without checking conditions.

questions.question: If wind speed increases from 10 m/s to 20 m/s, the total wind power density (P/A = ½ρV³) increases by a factor of:

feedback.correct: Correct. Power ∝ V³. Doubling V gives 2³ = 8× more power.
feedback.wrong: Incorrect. Wind power varies with V³ (velocity cubed). Doubling wind speed gives 2³ = 8 times more power.

questions.question: The Betz limit states that no turbine can extract more than ________% of available wind power.

feedback.correct: Correct. The Betz limit = 16/27 ≈ 59.3% — the theoretical maximum any turbine can achieve.
feedback.wrong: Incorrect. The Betz limit = 16/27 ≈ 59.3%. No physical turbine can extract more than this fraction of available wind power.

questions.question: Axial thrust on a wind turbine is the force that:
options: Spins the rotor blades
Pushes the turbine in the direction of wind flow — the force trying to topple the tower
Drives the generator to produce electricity
Lifts the turbine off its foundation

feedback.correct: Correct. Axial thrust is the horizontal force in the wind direction — what engineers must resist in tower and foundation design.
feedback.wrong: Incorrect. Axial thrust is the horizontal pushing force the wind exerts on the rotor — what tries to topple the tower.

questions.question: In the family biogas digester, the retention time determines:
options: How much gas is produced per day
The methane fraction of the biogas
The required digester volume — the tank must hold retention time days' worth of slurry at once
The operating temperature of the digester

feedback.correct: Correct. Vd = Vf × tr. If 0.2 m³ enters daily and stays 20 days, the tank needs 4 m³ capacity.
feedback.wrong: Incorrect. Retention time determines digester volume: Vd = Vf × tr.

questions.question: In Worked Example 9.2 (5 cows, tr = 20 days), the required digester volume Vd = ________ m³.
Why is biogas NOT pure methane, and why does this matter for the power formula E = η·Hm·Fm·Vb?
options: Biogas contains 20–40% CO₂ which releases no energy on combustion — Fm corrects for this by using only the combustible methane fraction
Biogas contains hydrogen which burns hotter than methane
Biogas contains water vapour which absorbs heat during combustion
Fm corrects for the efficiency of the digester, not the gas composition

feedback.correct: Correct. Biogas is 60–80% methane and 20–40% CO₂. Only methane contributes heat. Fm corrects for this.
feedback.wrong: Incorrect. Biogas contains 20–40% CO₂ which is inert (releases no energy). Fm selects only the combustible methane fraction.

questions.question: For the village biogas plant, gas supply is always calculated using winter production figures. Why?
options: Dung production from animals is lower in winter
Bacterial activity slows in cold weather — gas yield per kg of dung is lower in winter — this is the worst case for supply
The community uses more gas for heating in winter so demand is higher
Water availability for slurry mixing is limited in winter

feedback.correct: Correct. Cold weather slows bacterial fermentation — winter gives the lowest gas yield per kg of dung. Design for worst case.
feedback.wrong: Incorrect. Winter gas yield per kg of dung is lower because cold temperatures slow bacterial activity.

questions.question: In the village digester sizing, dung is mixed 1:1 with water and the slurry density is 1090 kg/m³. If dung per digester = 825 kg/day, the daily charge volume is:

feedback.correct: Correct. Both dung (825 kg) and equal water (825 kg) are included: (825+825)/1090 = 1.51 m³.
feedback.wrong: Incorrect. Both dung AND equal water by mass are mixed together. Total mass = 825+825 = 1650 kg.

questions.question: In Worked Example 9.3, each of the 4 village digesters has height H equal to diameter D. What is the value of D and H?
options: 2 metres
4 metres
6 metres
8 metres

feedback.wrong: Incorrect. Solving V = (π/4)D³ gives D ≈ 4m, H = D = 4m.
